items.prompt: OrderService takes an IEmailService in its constructor instead of doing `new SmtpEmailService()` inside. Why is that version easier to unit test?
items.answer: A test can pass in a fake IEmailService, so nothing is really sent, while new-ing SMTP locks in the real one
distractors: Constructor injection makes Send run faster, so the unit tests finish well before their timeout
Test projects reference interfaces rather than classes, so a concrete SmtpEmailService would not load there
The DI container skips real network calls by itself whenever the tests are running
items.explanation: The bug hunt: newing dependencies inside a class means you cannot swap in a test version or control its lifetime.

items.prompt: IEmailService is registered with `AddScoped<IEmailService, SmtpEmailService>()`. In a web app, two services resolved in the same HTTP request both depend on it. How many SmtpEmailService instances exist for that request?
items.answer: One: a scoped service is created once per request scope and shared within that scope
distractors: Two: each injection point in the request receives its own newly created instance
One for the whole application: created at startup and reused by each later request
One per thread: the count depends on how many threads happened to serve the request
items.explanation: Transient = new every time; Scoped = one per request/scope; Singleton = one for the app's lifetime.

items.prompt: A Singleton cache service takes the Scoped AppDbContext in its constructor. What goes wrong?
items.answer: It holds one scope's DbContext for the app's life: stale data, shared by requests, never disposed
distractors: Nothing goes wrong: the container hands the singleton a fresh DbContext on every single method call
Nothing bad: the container promotes AppDbContext to Singleton to match, the recommended setup
The singleton is silently downgraded to Scoped: it just loses its cached data each request
items.explanation: A captive dependency is a longer-lived service holding a shorter-lived one; scoped services are meant to be disposed at the end of their scope.

items.prompt: Why does the lesson recommend binding the AppSettings section to an AppOptions class with Configure<AppOptions> rather than reading `_config["AppSettings:MaxRetries"]` wherever it is needed?
items.answer: The section binds once to a typed class, so MaxRetries is an int and the key lives in one place
distractors: Configure<T> encrypts the bound section, so secrets can safely stay in appsettings.json
IConfiguration cannot read nested keys, so values inside AppSettings are unreachable without options
Options are baked in at compile time, so the section is not read again at app startup
items.explanation: GetSection navigates nested config; Configure<T> binds a section to a strongly typed class (the recommended Options pattern).

items.prompt: ApiClient receives its HttpClient through the constructor (IHttpClientFactory). What breaks if it instead did `using var http = new HttpClient();` inside every call?
items.answer: Each disposed client leaves its socket lingering, so heavy load can exhaust the available sockets
distractors: Nothing breaks; a new HttpClient per call is the recommended thread-safe pattern in .NET
A fresh HttpClient cannot send JSON bodies, so PostAsJsonAsync would stop working for the client
Disposing one HttpClient cancels the in-flight requests made by the app's other HttpClients
items.explanation: The lesson's first common mistake is creating a new HttpClient for every request (socket exhaustion); the second is not using IHttpClientFactory.

items.prompt: The API answers GET /users/42 with 404 Not Found. What does GetUserAsync(42) do?
items.answer: EnsureSuccessStatusCode throws an HttpRequestException: the 404 body is never returned
distractors: It returns the 404 error body as the user string: the HTTP call itself did not fail
It returns null: ReadAsStringAsync yields null for any error response it reads
GetAsync itself throws on any non-2xx status: EnsureSuccessStatusCode never even runs
items.explanation: GetAsync returns the response whatever its status; EnsureSuccessStatusCode is the line that throws when it is not 2xx.

items.prompt: A request for /home flows through the custom `app.Use` middleware and then the terminal `app.Run`. In what order do the console lines and the response body happen?
items.answer: "Request: /home" is logged, Run writes Hello, then after await next() "Response sent" is logged
distractors: "Response sent" is logged first, then "Request: /home", and after that Hello is written
Just "Request: /home" is logged: Run short-circuits, so code after await next() is skipped
Both lines are logged before Hello is written: Run executes after each Use delegate has returned
items.explanation: await next() passes control down the pipeline; code after it runs on the way back out. Run is terminal: it does not call further middleware.

items.prompt: Someone deletes the `await next();` line from the logging middleware. What happens to requests?
items.answer: It short-circuits there, so Run never executes and clients get an empty response, not Hello
distractors: ASP.NET Core calls the next middleware automatically once the delegate returns without calling it
The app fails at startup with an exception stating that every Use delegate must call next
The request is retried by the host until some middleware in the pipeline calls next
items.explanation: Middleware only continues the chain by calling next(); the bug hunt lists 'Not calling next()' and 'Short circuiting too early'.

items.prompt: Why does the lesson register UseAuthentication and UseAuthorization near the top, and what happens if authorization is placed after middleware that already produced the response?
items.answer: Middleware runs in registration order, so anything answering before auth skips the auth check
distractors: Order does not matter, as ASP.NET Core sorts built-in middleware into the correct order itself
Authorization placed later runs anyway and retroactively replaces the sent response with 401
The app refuses to start whenever UseAuthorization is not registered as the first middleware
items.explanation: 'Order matters': a short-circuiting component earlier in the pipeline means later middleware (like auth) never sees the request.

items.prompt: QueueProcessor checks `stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested` in its loop condition. Why does it also pass stoppingToken into `Task.Delay(1000, stoppingToken)`?
items.answer: So shutdown cancels the wait at once, instead of the loop sleeping on until the delay ends
distractors: Without a token Task.Delay never completes, so the loop would hang forever on the first wait
The token makes the delay exactly 1000 ms instead of approximately 1000 ms on a busy machine
The token restarts the loop automatically if the work inside it throws an unhandled exception
items.explanation: Respecting the cancellation token everywhere (loop check and awaited calls) gives clean, prompt shutdown; ignoring it causes abrupt shutdowns.

items.prompt: Why does OrderService log `LogInformation("Processing order {OrderId}", orderId)` instead of `LogInformation($"Processing order {orderId}")`?
items.answer: The template keeps OrderId as a named, queryable property, while interpolation bakes it into flat text
distractors: ILogger methods reject interpolated strings at compile time, so templates are required to build
The template binds {OrderId} by name to a local called OrderId, so it is protected from logging a wrong value
The template form encrypts the order id, so it does not appear in plain text in the log files
items.explanation: Structured logging with {Property}: placeholders are filled positionally from the arguments and kept as structured data.

items.prompt: How many test cases does the runner report for `Add_VariousInputs` as written?
items.answer: Two: a Theory runs once per InlineData row, (2, 3, 5) and (0, 0, 0)
distractors: One: both InlineData rows are checked together inside a single test case
Three: the runner creates one test case per method parameter
Zero: a Theory only runs when it is also marked with [Fact]
items.explanation: [Theory] + [InlineData] runs the test multiple times with different data, one case per row.

items.prompt: You add a `Discount` property to Product but never create or apply a migration. What happens the next time the app queries Products?
items.answer: EF's SQL selects the new column, but the table lacks it, so the query fails at runtime
distractors: EF adds the missing column to the table automatically the first time Products is queried
EF ignores the new property until a migration exists, so queries keep working unchanged
The project fails to compile until a migration for the model change has been added
items.explanation: Migrations keep the schema in step with the model; 'Forgetting to apply migrations' is one of the lesson's common mistakes.

items.front: EF bug hunt: why should DbContext not be registered as a singleton?
items.back: It is a unit of work that tracks entities and is not thread-safe; registered Scoped it lives for one request and is disposed at the end of the scope.

items.front: Listing 50 posts and reading post.Comments for each one runs 51 queries. Name the problem and the EF Core fix.
items.back: The N+1 query problem: one query for the list, then one per row for its related data. Load the related data up front with Include (or project with Select).

items.front: What does `await using var writer = new StreamWriter("log.txt", append: true);` guarantee, and what bug does it prevent?
items.back: The writer is disposed asynchronously (flushed and the file handle released) when the scope ends, even on exceptions; it prevents leaked handles and lost buffered writes.

items.front: A class takes IServiceProvider and calls GetService<IEmailService>() inside its methods. What anti-pattern is this and why is it bad?
items.back: Service locator: the real dependencies are hidden from the constructor, so tests and readers cannot see them and a missing registration fails only at runtime. Inject the dependencies; only the composition root knows concrete types.

items.front: Two IEmailSender implementations (SMTP and SendGrid) must coexist. What .NET 8 DI feature picks between them?
items.back: Keyed services: register with AddKeyedScoped<IEmailSender, SmtpEmailSender>("smtp") and resolve with GetRequiredKeyedService<IEmailSender>("smtp") (or [FromKeyedServices("smtp")]).
